entry.title: Aaron Levie (@levie)
entry.content:
Amazing outcome. Cursor executed the applied AI strategy flawlessly.
Most people completely underestimated the market size in AI coding. The biggest developer tool exits in history were on the order of low billions of dollars. And it was already assumed to be a heavily competitive and somewhat saturated space when they really got going.
Multiple mental models shattered near instantly. The market sizes for agentic coding was far larger than most realized. There was actually tons and tons of room to innovate between the user and the underlying model, and even on the model itself.
Cursor provided out the applied AI playbook by figuring out the right product shape for agentic coding work, acting as a neutral layer between models and the workflows, post training models for the areas that make most sense to drive down costs or improve performance, building out the right infra stack for the relevant workflows, building out a strong category-aligned GTM motion, and more.
Great set of lessons for anyone doing applied AI right now. We’re going to see a lot more of these.

entry.title: Madhu Guru (@realmadhuguru)
entry.content:
Making steam engines more efficient increased coal demand.
Higher-level languages made programming easier and resulted in far more software being built.
Spreadsheets made financial analysis cheaper and resulted in businesses doing far more analysis.
When the cost and complexity of a task falls, new use cases become economically viable.
AI + software engineering will likely follow the same pattern: far more software solving far more problems, including problems that were previously economically unviable.

entry.title: Peter Yang (@petergyang)
entry.content:
I was curious how X is fighting AI slop, so I looked at its open-source algorithm.
It has a behavioral model called TweetSpamBot that analyzes up to 512 recent account actions, looking at signals like posting bursts, quote-post behavior, timing, and normal browsing or dwell between actions.
The model is trained to recognize patterns such as:
→ TWEET_CREATE_BURST → QUOTE_TWEET_SPAMMER → CONTENT_AMPLIFIER
A high score on the above can feed into an account challenge but doesn't seem to downrank the slop posts themselves.
I think the gap here is that the model doesn’t read the actual post content.
So a sophisticated AI content mill can still post slop all day long:
1. Find viral posts 2. Quote tweet with the same template each time: hook → numbers → backstory → takeaway 3. Repeat 10+ times a day across unrelated topics
If @X doesn't want to become like LinkedIn, I think it should consider looking at accounts that repeatedly turn unrelated viral posts into the same templated quote tweet slop at high volume.
Right now the guardrails above are too easy to bypass.

entry.title: Claude Blog: Building intelligent apps for Apple platforms with Claude in the Foundation Models framework
entry.content: Today we're releasing Foundation Models framework support for Claude through a new Swift package that lets Apple developers use Apple's Foundation Models framework to call Claude for more complex workflows. Apple’s Foundation Models framework gives developers access to tap into models natively from Swift. It is very easy to use and can return typed Swift values through guided generation in as few as three lines of code. Developers can use this to tap into Apple’s on-device models for fast, local tasks like summarization or extraction. Developers can now use Apple’s Foundation Models framework to hand off to Claude when a request calls for multi-step reasoning, code generation, and more. Claude can also search the web for current information and execute code for data analysis. Stream Claude's response back into the same view.
